members.title: 打得够帅，也要打得够好：多人动作游戏《狩》试玩体验 x 开发团队采访

news.body:
11月25日，由腾讯魔方工作室自研的多人动作竞技新作《狩》，正式公布了首支宣传PV。
这是一款以近战动作为核心的多人竞技游戏。除了不同风格的角色与丰富的武器系统之外，游戏还准备了包括赛事模式（吃鸡玩法）、1V1、3V3在内的多种竞技玩法，并采用了颇具辨识度的街头潮流美术风格。从官方首次展示的内容来看，《狩》希望让玩家在激烈的对抗中打出华丽的连招，享受动作竞技带来的战斗乐趣。
而在游戏正式公布之前，我受邀参加了《狩》的线下媒体试玩会，提前体验到了这款作品。
在活动现场，官方邀请了不少游戏媒体、KOL以及UP主来到现场，除了安排大家亲自上手体验之外，还将参与者之间的对战搬到了这座擂台上。场地后方的大屏幕则实时播放着战斗画面，让其他人也能观看比赛。
这样的安排倒是很符合《狩》本身的气质。当两名玩家在擂台上展开较量，身后的大屏幕同步呈现出各种华丽的连招与激烈的攻防时，整个现场也有了几分动作竞技赛事的味道。即使只是站在一旁观看，也很容易被比赛的气氛所感染。
当然，看别人打得热闹是一回事，自己上手又是另一回事。
这次试玩，官方为我们提供了PC设备，我总共体验了大约两个小时，参与了四场比赛，其中包括两场三人组队的赛事模式，以及两场1V1对抗。在三排模式中，我的队友也都是受邀到场的其他媒体老师。并且在这四场比赛中，我还很有幸“吃了一次鸡”。
虽然总体的体验时间不算太长，但几场比赛下来，《狩》还是给我留下了比较深刻的印象。它的战斗节奏很快，玩家之间的交锋也相当紧张，再加上充满风格化的动作演出，让整个战斗过程显得十分热闹。
而在这些直观的感受之外，我觉得《狩》更值得聊一聊的，还是它的战斗系统。
对于一款以近战为核心的多人动作竞技游戏来说，战斗系统显然是它最重要的部分。在实际体验之后，我觉得《狩》比较有意思的地方，就是它把基础操作设计得相当简单：即使是第一次接触游戏的玩家，也能轻松地衔接不同招式，完成一套颇为华丽的连续攻击。
这次试玩中，我主要使用了刺剑、巨剑等武器。《狩》拥有主副武器机制，虽然不同武器的攻击动作和战斗节奏有所区别，但游戏的基础攻防关系并不复杂，主要围绕着【轻攻击】、【重攻击】和【破招攻击】三种招式展开。简单来说，三种攻击之间存在相互克制的关系，有点类似于我们熟悉的“猜拳”机制。
同时，《狩》还创新地将动作博弈体系融入技能设计之中，让玩家可以通过不同招式之间的选择与衔接完成攻防转换。一旦在攻防博弈中取得优势，玩家便可以顺势衔接后续招式，展开连续进攻。
这种设计让我在刚上手时感到非常轻松。相比一些需要记忆复杂指令的动作游戏，《狩》并没有设置太高的基础操作门槛，只要理解不同攻击之间的关系，就能够很快参与到战斗之中。
不过，随着对局的深入，我逐渐发现基础连段虽然不难掌握，但想要在与其他玩家的对抗中占据优势，仍然需要不少技巧。
其中让我印象比较深刻的就是“垫步取消”——通过垫步来取消掉招式的后摇，甚至能够中断招式。在几场实际对抗中，我能够明显感受到，熟练运用这类操作的玩家，往往能够更好地掌握战斗节奏。尤其是在1V1的情况下，双方的攻防转换非常快，如果只依靠基础攻击进行博弈，很容易被对手抓住机会。
对这种“容易上手，但不容易精通”的设计，开发团队在试玩会后的媒体答疑中也给出了具体的解释。
“首先，我们非常明确的目标就是我们的下限要够低，因为其实本身动作游戏相对而言门槛就是偏高的，我们又是做多人动作的，所以我们的第一个目标是要把门槛降低。”
按照制作组的说法，他们希望通过相对简单的底层战斗规则，让更多玩家能够快速理解游戏。在此基础上，再通过不同的角色、武器与芯片，进一步提高游戏的操作上限。这也与我在试玩过程中的感受比较一致——《狩》并不要求玩家在开始游戏之前，就花费大量时间练习复杂的连招，而是让大家先体验战斗的乐趣，再随着对游戏的熟悉，逐渐掌握更多的操作。
除了基础操作之外，《狩》在战斗演出方面也下了不少功夫，其中最有代表性的，就是游戏中的Shotime机制。
在实际对抗中，当玩家通过克制对手的攻击触发“Shotime”时，游戏便会进入一段特殊的战斗演出。伴随着夸张的视觉效果，对手会被大幅击飞，玩家也能顺势展开后续攻击。整个过程一气呵成，无论是动作表现还是实际操作，都有着不错的爽快感。
而这也正是制作组反复强调的“战斗秀，战斗爽”——制作组说，“为什么叫‘战斗秀’？首先是符合我们秀场的概念，其次动作游戏天然的优势就是可以打得很帅。先不说我们能不能打赢，但是一定能打得很帅。”
不过，强调“连续攻击”与“华丽的连招”，势必也会带来一些问题：例如当一名玩家被对手连续压制时，可能会有较长一段时间无法重新掌握主动权。
在媒体答疑中，也有其他媒体针对受击硬直和连招持续时间提出了疑问。对此制作组解释说，《狩》加入了相应的脱身机制，让玩家有机会打断对方的连续攻击。但与此同时，他们也希望保留足够的连招时间，让进攻方能够享受到动作游戏带来的爽快感。
我觉得这也是《狩》在未来值得关注的部分。毕竟，一款多人竞技游戏既要让进攻方打得尽兴，也需要给防守方留下合理的应对空间。尤其是随着玩家逐渐掌握各种进阶技巧，双方对于攻防时机的判断、招式之间的博弈，以及脱身后的应对，都将变得更加重要。
这些建立在基础操作之上的变化，究竟能够让《狩》的战斗衍生出多少可能性，这正是我对这款游戏后续表现最期待的地方了。
除了1V1对抗之外，这次我还体验了两场三人组队的赛事模式。
相比单人对决，三排模式下需要考虑的事情显然要多得多。玩家不仅需要应对眼前的对手，还要随时留意队友与其他敌人的位置。尤其是当几名玩家同时参与近战时，各种攻击与移动动作交织在一起，战场上的情况往往瞬息万变，也让整场对抗变得更加紧张。
《狩》中的不同角色拥有各自的技能与战斗定位，玩家还可以通过拾取不同武器、选择战斗芯片调整自己的策略。按照制作组的介绍，这些系统不仅能够提高个人操作的上限，也能让玩家通过不同的阵容搭配，在团队战斗中发挥各自的作用。
在谈到团队配合时，制作组举了一个例子：当队友遭到对手的“Shotime”攻击时，其他玩家可以通过抱摔打断这一过程，帮助队友脱离困境。制作组希望通过类似的机制，让玩家在个人操作之外，还能通过团队协作获得更多战术选择。
“团队之间有配合，互相之间的配合其实就是上限比较高的事情，我们只要提供土壤和空间。”制作组这样解释道。
不过，由于这次试玩时间有限，而且队友也都是刚刚接触游戏的其他媒体老师，因此我并没有深入研究不同角色与芯片之间的组合。几局玩下来，我更多感受到的还是个人操作的重要性。尤其是在多人混战中，如果无法熟练掌握一些进阶技巧，即使有队友在身边，也很容易被对手抓住机会一套带走。
当然，三排模式的乐趣也不只是几个人凑在一起战斗。除了玩家之间的配合，如何在整场比赛中获得更多资源，同样是游戏的重要组成部分。而在这方面，《狩》表现出了相当明确的设计倾向，那就是——鼓励玩家主动交战。
玩家需要在地图中寻找物资、强化装备，并通过击败其他队伍获得战利品。在这次试玩中，我能明显感受到整个比赛的节奏比较快，而战斗结束后的搜刮又能够帮助队伍进一步提高实力，让玩家有理由不断寻找新的对手。
制作组在媒体答疑中也谈到了这一点。他们表示，地图中的决斗场、空投等地点都会提供较为丰厚的资源，而这些区域通常也是战斗最激烈的地方。
按照他们的说法，就是：“打架是一定会让你越打越富的。”
除此之外，游戏还设计了多种复活机制，尽可能减少玩家因为一次失误，就提前结束整场比赛的情况。制作组希望通过这些设计，降低玩家在交战时的顾虑，让大家能够更加积极地投入战斗。
而要保持这样的节奏，角色的移动能力同样重要。在这次试玩中，我对《狩》的移动表现相当满意。游戏中的角色拥有很强的机动性，可以利用跑酷、跳跃以及光链拖拽等方式迅速穿越地图。尤其是光链，不仅能够帮助玩家快速接近目标，甚至还可以直接锁住敌人，在追击过程中发挥很大的作用。
不过，较强的移动能力也让我产生了另一个疑问：当玩家决定撤退时，又该如何摆脱对手的追击？在媒体答疑中，也有其他媒体提出了类似的问题，认为目前游戏中的追击方似乎拥有比较明显的优势。
对此，制作组也坦言：“现阶段我确实也认为追击方的能力会更强一些，但是我觉得通过一些参数或者是机制是能解决的。”他们还提到，游戏中已经提供了一些抵抗追击的操作与芯片能力，只不过想要熟练运用这些机制，仍然需要玩家具备一定的操作技巧。
对于一款以近战为核心的多人竞技游戏来说，什么时候主动交战、什么时候选择撤退，本身就是玩家需要考虑的重要问题。而《狩》通过较强的移动能力，以及鼓励玩家争夺资源的玩法设计，让双方之间的交锋变得更加频繁。
这或许也是我在这次试玩中感受最明显的地方：整场比赛始终保持着紧张的节奏，而游戏中的各种机制又在不断鼓励玩家主动寻找对手，让一场接着一场的激烈交锋，成为整个赛事模式最有吸引力的部分。
除了战斗系统与大地图玩法之外，《狩》还有一个相当鲜明的特点，就是它所强调的“街头潮流”风格。
从角色的服装、武器设计，到移动方式与攻击动作，《狩》融入了不少现代街头文化的元素。无论是滑板、跑酷，还是使用光链追击对手时的动作表现，都让游戏呈现出了与传统武侠、奇幻题材动作游戏不同的面貌。是那些带有表演性质的动作细节，也在这次试玩中给我留下了非常深刻的印象。
他们表示在最初确定角色设计方向时，他们就希望《狩》中的角色能够拥有比较自然的街头穿搭，而不是一群穿着夸张服装的Cosplayer。因此，在服装剪裁和整体造型上，团队会相对克制一些，再通过鲜艳的色彩与不同的搭配方式，突出角色年轻、富有活力的特点。
除了外观设计之外，制作组还希望让角色的动作本身也带有潮流感。
他们在采访中举了一个挺有意思的例子：在传统动作游戏中，一名使用巨剑的角色可能会在攻击结束后，直接将武器收回到背后。但在《狩》中，制作组则会加入一些额外的表演动作，例如让角色用脚踢一下巨剑，再顺势将它扛起来。类似的设计还体现在武器切换、跑酷和滑板等动作中。按照制作组的说法，他们希望玩家在正常游玩的过程中，就能自然地做出一些颇具观赏性的动作，而不需要刻意追求表演效果。
这其实也体现了制作组对于“秀场”的理解。在采访中，他们还专门解释了《狩》这个名字的由来。一方面，“狩”很容易让人联想到狩猎，与游戏的吃鸡玩法相呼应；另一方面，“狩”的拼音“Shou”又与英文“Show”发音相近，这也是制作组希望突出“秀场”概念的原因之一。
对于《狩》来说，所谓的“秀”，并不只是通过华丽的画面来包装游戏，而是希望玩家在日常操作中，也能展现出具有观赏性的动作。无论是Shotime的特殊演出，还是各种移动与攻击动作中的细节，制作组在这方面的用心打磨，都能看出制作组在这方面的用心打磨，让“秀”的概念贯穿于玩家的整个游戏体验之中。
在试玩会后的媒体答疑中，有一个媒体老师提出的问题给我留下了特别深刻的印象：如今的多人竞技游戏市场，已经有了大量成熟的MOBA与射击游戏，为什么魔方工作室还会选择以近战动作为核心，开发这样一款新的竞技产品？
这句话听起来有些简单，却体现了团队对于自身开发能力的十足信心。按照制作组的介绍，魔方过去已经积累了丰富的动作PVP开发经验，因此也希望发挥自身的优势，将这些经验运用到一款全新的多人竞技游戏之中。
不过，从过去相对熟悉的横版动作游戏转向全3D视角的多人动作PVP，这并不是一件容易的事情。制作组坦言，团队在开发初期经历了大量的调研与迭代，才逐渐形成了如今的游戏形态。
而对于市场竞争的问题，制作组也给出了另一个挺有意思的观点——“现在没有一个非常高DAU的动作产品出现，那何尝不是动作游戏这个品类的机会所在呢？”在他们看来，如今的多人竞技市场虽然已经有了不少成熟产品，但这并不意味着动作游戏就没有机会。如果能够让更多玩家接受多人动作竞技的玩法，或许就有机会吸引一批新的用户。
这也解释了为什么《狩》会如此重视操作门槛。制作组希望通过相对简单的基础规则，让更多玩家快速理解战斗系统，再逐渐研究角色、武器与芯片之间的搭配，在不断熟悉游戏的过程中提高自己的竞技水平。
另外，《狩》还计划支持PC与移动端账号共通，但两个平台采用分开的匹配环境。当然，这次我实际体验的只有PC版本，因此对于移动端的操作表现，以及不同平台之间的体验差异，暂时还无法做出评价。而在商业化方面，制作组也明确表示，不会对角色本身设置付费门槛，而是主要围绕角色与武器外观等内容展开。
回顾这次的试玩活动，《狩》给我留下了相当不错的印象——从简单直观的基础战斗规则，到爽快且充满表现力的Shotime演出；从灵活自由的移动方式，到鼓励玩家主动交战的赛事模式……这些设计不仅让我能够很快融入游戏，也让整个战斗过程始终保持着紧张而明快的节奏。
当然，两小时内的四场比赛还不足以让我完全理解这款游戏。无论是不同武器之间的平衡、角色与芯片的搭配，还是成熟队伍之间的团队协作，都还有不少值得进一步研究的内容。不过，从目前的体验来看，我认为《狩》已经展现出了一种全新的游戏体验。
如今，玩家的游戏时间早已被大量成熟产品占据，对于一款全新的多人竞技游戏来说，想要让大家愿意尝试，并且长期投入其中，这本身就是一个不小的挑战。而《狩》选择的近战动作竞技方向，虽然并非全新的玩法，但它所呈现出的战斗节奏、操作方式与街头潮流风格，还是让我感受到了一些不同于传统格斗和“大逃杀”游戏的乐趣。
至于《狩》最终能够走到哪一步，现在还很难下结论。但至少在这次试玩结束后，我已经开始期待下一次与其他玩家交手的机会了。2027年1月，《狩》将开启首测测试，想体验试玩的各位玩家，可以前往官方渠道进行预约。

news.body:
GTA 6 Becomes the Biggest Launch in PlayStation History
Rockstar's blockbuster attracted more than 39 million unique players on PlayStation and set several platform records.
In case you missed it
Related news
Grand Theft Auto 6 has become the biggest launch in PlayStation history, attracting more than 39 million unique players and setting records for concurrent players and newly connected PS5 consoles.
Sony Interactive Entertainment shared launch data from November 19 to November 22 in a blog post. According to the report, GTA 6 surpassed previous records across multiplayer, free-to-play, and single-player titles.
PlayStation recorded the largest number of newly connected PS5 consoles in a single day since the console's launch, outside the end-of-year holiday season, which suggests many players bought a PS5 just for the game. GTA 6 was also the first game played on 70% of newly connected PS5 consoles. Players logged 683 million hours of gameplay in GTA 6, averaging 17.4 hours per player.
"These are just a few ways we've seen our PlayStation community come together around this incredible moment in gaming, and we're excited to see how you continue to build and share new memories and experiences in the months ahead," the post reads.
According to Sensor Tower data, about 75% of the copies sold across all platforms by the morning of launch were for PlayStation. The platform even confirmed a service disruption on November 18, hours before GTA 6 began unlocking around the world.
Grand Theft Auto 6 became the biggest entertainment launch in history, generating an estimated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales during its first 24 hours. Before launch, it had already sold 32.5 million units across all platforms. As previously reported, GTA 6 earned more than Avengers: Endgame, the highest-grossing film in history. The 2019 movie earned approximately $2.94 billion worldwide during its theatrical run, and GTA 6 surpassed that number by around $850 million in a single day.

news.title: Is your data telling you the whole story?
news.summary_raw: Data fragmentation hides the full player picture. See what it costs UA and monetization teams and which MMP, GA and IAP signals to connect to Unity Vector.

members.title: Is your data telling you the whole story?

news.body:
Is your data telling you the whole story?
UA and monetization teams don’t have a data shortage. They have a data fragmentation problem. Spend, installs, in-game behavior, ad revenue, and in-app purchases (IAP) sit in separate platforms that don’t talk to each other, so no one sees the full picture. That gap can lead to bad calls on bids, budgets, and creative.
Here’s what data fragmentation costs UA and monetization teams, and which signals to connect to Unity Vector, the AI foundation of Unity Ads.
Why should you be concerned about data fragmentation?
Data fragmentation is when player data is spread across separate tools that don’t share a common view.
Studios have plenty of data. But with the player journey scattered across mobile measurement partners (MMPs), ad revenue and IAP systems, analytics tools,, and SDKs, each tool shows only part of it: where players come from, what they buy, how they behave.
Because those pieces sit in silos, optimization engines rarely see the whole picture. The impact can be an incomplete view of player value, missing context across the player journey, and measurement and optimization blind spots.
Marc Wofford, Lead Analyst at Kooapps, says it best: “...Multiple sources aren’t inherently bad. The problem is fragmentation, when those sources are difficult to reconcile and activate. Bringing them together in a way that’s actually usable is what makes the difference.”
Incomplete view of player value
When conversion data is split across disconnected systems, your ad platform’s optimization engine sees only part of what players do, which can limit its understanding of player value. In contrast, feeding unified conversion events back to the platform lets it optimize toward users who actually converted, giving it a more accurate signal to learn from.
Missing context across the player journey
Viewing players in isolated silos misses the reality that conversion is rarely driven by one touchpoint alone. When those touchpoints live in separate systems that don't share data, studios may struggle to understand the broader player journey and what drives revenue.
When data tells different stories
Siloed data limits comparison across sources. Each source tells its own version of what happened, and without a way to reconcile them, it’s difficult to know which picture is the most complete.
Benefits of a strong data foundation
Fragmentation limits how well an optimization engine can learn from your players. So what do you gain by connecting more signals?
Clearer decisions
Richer, connected data can fill blind spots and add granularity, turning a single flat data point into a more detailed picture of exactly which moment, action, or player segment actually drove the outcome. With that detail, you can act on what worked instead of guessing. Wofford recounts:
“Our internal analytics give us the flexibility to quickly add new data points without heavy planning or approval. That freedom lets us be genuinely experimental about what we log, and it pays off. Some of those events turn out to be strong value signals, real insights we wouldn’t have caught otherwise, and finding ways to translate them into our optimization platforms is where a lot of the upside is.”
Better optimization
Agreement across sources acts as a built-in check on accuracy. Cross-checking sources can help teams identify discrepancies before using the data for optimization.
Stronger long-term performance
A more complete, connected set of signals can improve prediction accuracy over time, giving optimization engines like Unity Vector more to learn from as campaigns scale.
As Prince Yang, Director of User Acquisition at Dobest, put it:
“After improving our data postback setup, Unity Vector was able to leverage a more comprehensive set of signals - including installs, retention, ad revenue, in-app purchase revenue, and ROAS - to help the model identify high-value users more accurately. Since launching the D28 ROAS campaign, we have also seen clear improvements in medium- to long-term campaign stability, user quality, and return on ad spend.”*
Why isn’t mobile measurement partner (MMP) data enough?
A common misconception is that MMP data and Google Analytics (GA) data are redundant. If you’ve already connected MMP data, events, and IAP data, you may think adding GA data is overkill. But this misunderstanding can prevent studios from getting the full picture they need to make informed decisions. Here’s what you can glean from each of these sources:
MMP data
MMP data tells you where an install came from (which campaign, network, and creative drove it) and what it was worth. Typically, an MMP only carries the events you’ve mapped, so it’s usually a small subset of behavior.
Google Analytics
GA captures the in-game events you log, typically a broader set than the events mapped to your MMP. Without it, a studio can see that a valuable player converted, but may have limited visibility into why, which is exactly the kind of context needed to explain, replicate, or fix the pattern, rather than just observe it. Adding GA signals enriches your existing MMP data, giving Unity Vector behavioral context alongside attribution, which may help it better understand your most valuable players.
To build a more complete picture of player behavior and value, Wonder Kingdom is integrating both MMP and GA data into Unity Vector.
As Marketing Director Shuai Tang puts it: “We have been improving our data infrastructure step by step. Our current focus is integrating MMP attribution data, monetization data, and in-app behavioral data from Google Analytics into Unity Vector. MMP data gives us visibility into attribution and key conversions, while Google Analytics helps us understand the user journey after entering the app.
By combining these signals, we can build a more complete picture of user value and provide Vector with richer signals for model learning.”
Signal source
What it tells you
Where an install came from (campaign, network, and creative pack), plus the value and cost of that install. Covers install signals and mapped post-install events.
What it typically can’t tell you
Behavior beyond the events that were mapped which level they got stuck on, what path they took before churning, or which feature they engaged with right before converting.
What it tells you
Broader in-game behavior and the user journey after they enter the app. Explains why a valuable player converted.
What it typically can’t tell you
Doesn’t replace attribution data from your MMP. GA complements it with additional behavioral and engagement context from the player journey.

Strengthening the value of your signals
When it comes to performance data, it’s not about any particular signal in itself. MMP data is an important piece of the puzzle, and so are GA, runtime data, IAP, and other signals. news.title: How Unimora is inspiring the next generation of aged care professionals through VR, built with Unity
news.summary_raw: Unimora, built with Unity, lets students experience both sides of aged care in VR to inspire care careers. A Unity for Humanity 2026 Honourable Mention.

members.title: How Unimora is inspiring the next generation of aged care professionals through VR, built with Unity

news.body:
How Unimora is inspiring the next generation of aged care professionals through VR, built with Unity
Subarna Ganguly Marshall - Unity
A student puts on a VR headset and becomes Joyce, an older woman living independently at home. Across the room, everything looks clear. Up close, the world is a blur. Joyce reaches for her phone and knocks it onto the floor, and her legs make her stop before she can pick it up.
Then the perspective shifts. The student is now Grace, Joyce’s aged care worker, arriving at the door with a new pair of glasses.
In a few minutes, the student has experienced both sides of care: what it feels like to need support, and what it takes to give it with respect and genuine connection.
That’s the vision behind Unimora, a virtual reality career-exploration experience from Australian immersive learning company Mindflight7, built with Unity, and recognized as an honorable mention in the Unity for Humanity Awards 2026.
Unimora challenges the narrow stereotype many young people hold about aged care work, also known as elder care or senior care. It aims to show the purpose, connection, and emotional value within the profession, from inside an interactive, story-driven virtual environment rather than a brochure or presentation.
Challenging barriers and stereotypes
Mindflight7’s first idea was a training simulation. Early conversations with industry professionals and students changed that. Bo Jiang, general manager of the aged care workforce division at Jim’s Group, a registered care provider in Australia, explained that few people enter aged care by plan, and that those who stay are the ones who find purpose in the work.
Students revealed the other half of the problem: virtually none had considered aged care as a career, and those who had saw it as difficult and exhausting.
Those challenges are part of the job, and Unimora doesn’t hide them, but they aren’t the whole picture. So the team shifted from skills training to what Mindflight7 calls “career tasting”: helping young people understand what the work feels like, why it matters, and what kind of person might find it rewarding.
Experiencing care from both perspectives
Unimora is a short, classroom-friendly experience, long enough for students to form an emotional connection and make meaningful decisions.
As virtual reality character Grace, students use hand interactions for small, everyday actions, such as clearing clothing that obstructs Joyce’s walking frame or moving a cup away from the edge of a table. They show that quality care often comes from noticing the details that keep someone safe and independent at home.
When Grace offers the new glasses, the student, back in Joyce’s view, must look at Grace and nod to give permission. Their conversation reveals the relationship behind the care: Joyce knows Grace’s family, and Grace knows Joyce’s history and enjoys her company.
The judgment and connection behind the work
At the heart of Unimora is a seemingly ordinary decision. Joyce is getting ready for an annual lunch, and the community bus arrives in fifteen minutes. Students choose how Grace responds: pick the clothes to save time, explain the time pressure and let Joyce decide, or let her choose without mentioning the bus. There’s no flashing “correct” answer, only the tension between efficiency, autonomy, and informed choice that care workers navigate every day.
If Joyce is allowed to choose, she picks a blue scarf her late husband, Arthur, bought her forty years earlier. In the mirror, the scene shifts into a memory: her younger self wearing the same scarf, with Arthur standing behind her. The scarf isn’t just clothing. It carries Joyce’s identity, her history, and her connection to someone she has lost, and it shows students why this kind of care can be meaningful for both the person receiving it and the person providing it.
The experience closes with the message: “Care helps people keep living life on their own terms. You are the one who keeps the music playing.” A short reflection based on each student’s choices follows, with no scores or right-or-wrong labels, ending on one question: “Could you see yourself doing work like this?”
Building an immersive experience with Unity
Unity is at the center of how Mindflight7 builds Unimora and its wider library of immersive learning experiences.
Mindflight7 works with external development partners to deliver more than ten new VR experiences to schools each year, an output it expects to roughly double as AI becomes more integrated into its workflow. It leads the learning and interaction design, while its technical lead works inside partner teams to turn those designs into production-ready applications.
For this distributed model, Unity is the team’s go-to VR platform. The size and maturity of the Unity XR ecosystem make it easier to bring new developers onto a project without introducing an unfamiliar stack. Its component-based architecture makes it simpler to divide work across interaction, UI, environments, visual effects, and gameplay systems. Rapid prototyping suits educational VR, which benefits from frequent testing and refinement rather than long development cycles.
In Unimora, Unity powers the full real-time experience: the first-person shifts between Joyce and Grace, hand-based interactions, environmental objects, character animation, UI prompts, and the branching decisions that shape each student’s final reflection.
The team also developed custom shaders, including effects that represent changes in Joyce’s eyesight, and a real-time mirror solution built to run within the performance constraints of standalone VR headsets. The mirror became a key storytelling device in the scene where Joyce sees her younger self and Arthur, and achieving it convincingly on that hardware meant carefully balancing visual quality against rendering performance.
AI-assisted development is another reason Mindflight7 is deepening its work with Unity. Developers on its projects have found Unity easy to integrate into AI-enabled workflows. MCP-based integrations, and more recently Unity CLI workflows, give AI systems more direct access to a project’s structure and state, shortening the cycle between idea, implementation, testing, and revision.
What’s next for Unimora
Unimora is moving through real-world testing, from an internal alpha to a partner-facing beta, before school pilots gather student feedback. Mindflight7’s target is a 30% increase in positive career perception among participating students.
It will then reach high school students through Mindflight7’s in-school programs, including a new program focused on empathy and its existing healthcare careers program, and be offered to its 100+ XR Lab partner schools. Unimora is still at the start of its journey, but its approach shows how immersive experiences could help change how young people see care as a career.
Inspiring a more compassionate future of care
Unimora reflects the core mission of Unity for Humanity: using real-time 3D technology to address meaningful social challenges.
By letting students experience both receiving and providing care, and showing why a choice as small as a scarf can matter, Mindflight7 is doing more than introducing a potential career. It’s helping a new generation see aging differently, and recognize the role they could play in building a more skilled, compassionate, and sustainable future of care. It’s a poignant reminder that technology is at its best when it helps us understand one another a little better.

news.title: Access Asset Store and AI Generators using the Unity CLI
news.summary_raw: The Unity CLI and Asset Store lets coding agents search the store, pull single prefabs from packs, and generate missing assets with 60+ AI models.

members.title: Access Asset Store and AI Generators using the Unity CLI

news.body:
Access Asset Store and AI Generators using the Unity CLI
Your Coding Agent Can Now Access the Unity Asset Store
Today, we’re excited to announce that we’re making it easy and seamless for the AI tool of your choice to find, select, download, and import assets from the Unity Asset Store directly into your Unity projects. Imagine asking your agent to block out a forest clearing. It needs a pine tree, and your project doesn’t have one. So your agent goes and gets one. It searches the Asset Store, finds a tree in the right style, downloads that single model (not the 2 GB environment pack it came in), and drops it into your scene. You didn’t open a browser, and you didn’t import a thing.
This is possible because now the Unity CLI connects coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, and Google Antigravity to the Unity Asset Store and 60+ AI asset generators, so an agent can find, download, or generate assets directly into a Unity project.
It’s just one of the updates we’re announcing today, as we continue to deliver tools that help meet you where you work.
Grab one prefab, not the whole pack
You’ll now also be able to choose individual assets from an asset pack instead of having to download the entire pack for free assets or for those you already own. That’s because today we’re also excited to release the Asset Library plugin which combines with the Unity CLI to break up the old .unitypackage format, so individual prefabs show up when you need them. If all you need is one wooden barrel, you can now get just one wooden barrel, not a 650 MB medieval props pack to dig through.
The Asset Library plugin lets you describe what you want in plain language, find it, and drag it into your scene. Only the files that asset needs get downloaded, and import and file management happen automatically.
You also get data the Asset Store never showed before, like triangle count and animation rigging, so you can tell whether an asset is production ready before it touches your project.
Can’t find it? Your agent can make it
Some assets don’t exist yet. The exact sprite, a 3D model in a style nothing on the store matches, a sound effect too specific to have ever been recorded. And it’s also possible there isn’t an artist on your team. Starting today, your coding agent can use AI generators to create the assets you can’t find or have an artist create. These generators are also available through the Unity CLI, so that you can easily generate artifacts if you need to.
One command gets you sprites, 3D models, sound effects, and more, plus edits like background removal and upscaling. You can pick from 60+ models, and quotes are free, so you see the price before you spend any credits.
Every generated file records its model, its prompt, and its cost. Months later, when someone asks where a file came from, you have the answer.
It also makes a good placeholder. If the forest clearing needs a sound today and your artist is recording the real one next month, your agent fills the gap now. You can even ask your agent to pull up the file’s record so you know what to replace later.
One Unity login for all of it
Sign in once with the Unity ID you already have. The Asset Store and all 60+ generation models are part of your Unity account and the plan you’re associated with which comes with AI credits. When your agent searches the store or asks for a quote, it acts as you, with your entitlements and your spend. There’s no second account to create and nothing extra to set up for each model.
And you keep the agent you like. It reaches the store and the generators through the same Unity CLI it already uses to work with the Editor.
We want to meet you where you already work, and that means giving you more choice in how you build with Unity.
How can you get started today?
The Asset Store in the CLI and AI Generators in the CLI are both in open beta. The Asset Store CLI access to free assets is available to anyone. The AI Generators with CLI are part of Unity's AI tools and included on all Unity’s paid plans and use the credit allocation that comes with your plan.
Documentation for the Asset Store in the CLI is here, and documentation for the AI generators is here.
Tell us what you think. We can’t wait to see what you build!

news.title: 莫斯科游戏节在中国正式启动
news.summary_raw: 首届莫斯科游戏节在华启动，11月21日至25日上海五家网鱼网吧开放试玩十款本地化俄产精选游戏，活动压轴为中俄国际游戏开发马拉松。

members.title: 莫斯科游戏节在中国正式启动

news.body:
俄罗斯游戏产业正突破中国展会场馆的传统边界。上海玩家首次在全市各地的网吧中亲身体验俄罗斯开发的电子游戏。
11月21日至25日，中国大型连锁网吧品牌“网鱼”（WanYoo）旗下五家门店的顾客，将有机会试玩由莫斯科视频游戏与动画集群（Moscow Video Games and Animation Cluster）入驻企业及合作伙伴带来的十款精选游戏。此次活动是首届在华举办的“莫斯科游戏节”的重要组成部分。所有参展游戏均针对中国市场进行了本地化适配，其中部分作品甚至在中国正式发行前便提前亮相。游戏节将于11月28日至30日以一场“莫斯科—中国”国际游戏开发马拉松收尾，届时来自两国的游戏开发者将以线上远程协作的方式共同参与。
俄罗斯开发者首次直接将作品带入网吧场景，让玩家能够亲自上手体验游戏玩法、熟悉操作机制。入选上海游戏节活动的十款游戏项目，均是经过精心挑选，旨在契合当地玩家社群的兴趣偏好。
莫斯科创意产业局副总经理阿纳斯塔西娅·雷布金娜表示：“中国是俄罗斯游戏最大的出口市场，莫斯科游戏工作室三分之一的出口合同都流向这里。我们很高兴能在此展示全新项目，其中许多作品尚未在海外发布。这些作品的背后，是拥有强大团队、先进技术和独特创意解决方案的成熟俄罗斯游戏产业。通过网吧推广计划，更多中国玩家有机会接触到莫斯科工作室的成果。我们希望此次游戏节能进一步加强两国游戏社群之间的联系，并促进商业合作的发展。”
中国国际文化交流中心（CICEC）专家委员会成员赵旭指出：“如今，电子游戏已成为现代文化的重要组成部分。在莫斯科展区，最吸引我的首先是其对游戏题材的巧妙选择。俄罗斯游戏开发者与中国同行一样，都高度珍视并深耕自身的文化底蕴。当前，上海与莫斯科已跻身全球最具活力的游戏产业高地。我认为，双方合作前景十分广阔。为积极响应莫斯科的这一倡议，若能在俄罗斯首都举办中国电子游戏节，将是一件大有裨益的盛事。期待业界同仁能鼎力支持这一提议。”中国国际文化交流中心专家委员会委员赵旭表。”
莫斯科代表团带来的新品包括：WATT Studio开发的动作砍杀游戏《公主》（TSAREVNA. Age of Tales），其战斗系统融合了古典芭蕾元素；Antelus Games推出的海洋蒸汽朋克冒险游戏《海行者传奇》（Sea Walker Saga），结合角色扮演、海盗战斗与海洋探索玩法；同一工作室还带来了合作动作游戏《猫之战》（Cat's Wars），玩家可操控武装猫咪展开激战；Crumple Studios的作品《HomeWave》则将故事背景设定在一个虚拟操作系统内部。
此外，deep corp.开发的恐怖游戏《爷爷》（Deda）要求玩家从疯癫祖父的家中逃脱；Oxygen Chick推出的神秘冒险游戏《坩埚旅馆》（Cauldron Inn）邀请玩家探索一家阴郁的童话风格酒店；Halfwaypixel的模拟游戏《女仆搬运箱》（MAID MOVING BOXES）中，主角是一位安卓女仆及其无人机助手，任务是往船上装载箱子；Vampire Squid的合作动作游戏《嘎嘎猎人》（Quack Hunters）围绕猎杀变异动物以拯救被外星人绑架的山羊展开；Terrabyte Games的益智游戏《Pawsweeper》则借鉴“扫雷”玩法，玩家需要为收容所的猫咪清除跳蚤和蜱虫。
Hanuman Games推出的家庭冒险游戏《托托之旅》（Toto’s Journey）是唯一一款已登陆Steam平台并在欧美玩家群体中引发关注的参展新作。游戏主人公是一只名叫托托的小狗，它正在寻找回家的路。
网鱼网吧代表评论道：“我们很高兴，网鱼能够成为首届莫斯科游戏节在中国举办的合作伙伴之一。俄罗斯文化和神话故事一直对中国玩家有着独特的吸引力，因此我相信，这次带来的莫斯科游戏新作不仅会吸引我们俱乐部的老玩家，也会吸引不少专门为了体验这些新游戏而来的朋友。”
本届莫斯科游戏节将以“莫斯科—中国”国际游戏开发马拉松作为压轴活动。11月28日至30日的三天时间里，十支莫斯科团队与十支中国团队将联合开发新游戏原型。马拉松活动采用混合模式进行：线下部分设在莫斯科视频游戏与动画集群，线上部分则允许参与者远程接入。
本次参展的俄罗斯游戏项目均来自莫斯科视频游戏与动画集群的入驻企业及合作伙伴，该集群也是莫斯科游戏节的主办方。自2025年11月成立以来，该集群已迅速跻身全球最具竞争力的游戏产业枢纽前三名，与上海徐汇游戏产业带及阿布扎比AD Gaming Hub并列。
尽管莫斯科集群的面积仅为其他领先者的五分之一左右，但目前已汇聚超过70家企业，推进着250多个游戏项目。
部分参展游戏此前已在2026年11月21日至22日于上海举行的WePlay Expo展会的俄罗斯展区亮相。初步反馈显示，这些新品引起了中国观众的浓厚兴趣。如今，展会观众正期待它们在上海市内网吧的正式上线。
莫斯科游戏节由莫斯科视频游戏与动画集群主办，属于“莫斯科游戏出口”（Moscow Game Export）国际推广计划的一部分。2026年，莫斯科游戏工作室已先后参加在中国、日本、巴西、马来西亚和新加坡举办的行业活动。在2026年上海ChinaJoy展会上，12家莫斯科公司向中国观众展示了21个游戏项目，其中18个为全球首发。
背景资料：
莫斯科创意产业局（ACI）是莫斯科市文化局下属的创意产业发展机构，为电子游戏、动画、设计、当代艺术、出版等创意领域的企业与专业人士提供支持，并助力其产品开拓俄罗斯及国际市场。
莫斯科电子游戏与动画集群是推动电子游戏与动画产业发展的专项平台，于2025年11月成立。目前已有 70 余家企业入驻，正在推进的项目超过 250 个。该集群于2025年11月开业，是全球首个视频游戏和动画内容开发的全流程基础设施。在5.5万平方米的区域内，集中了制作视频游戏和动画所需的一切设施：动作捕捉工作室、录音棚、摄影测量工作室、审片室、电竞竞技场、讲堂和办公空间。集群内拥有俄罗斯最大的媒体屏幕，面积达800平方米。目前，已有60多家视频游戏和动画公司成为集群入驻企业，它们共同为俄罗斯及海外市场开发近170个项目。

发行、代理商杰仕登今日正式宣布，旗下首款自研动作 RPG Roguelike 游戏《定海》将于 12 月 3 日于STEAM平台正式发售！
《定海》是一款以「山海经」与「大禹治水」为背景的东方奇幻游戏。融合了动作RPG要素与Roguelike架构；加上流畅爽快的双武器战斗系统与史诗般的叙事，引领玩家展开壮阔的神话冒险！
培育自身能力，勇闯山海经神话世界
《定海》结合了动作RPG与Roguelike的元素，除了通过多种类武器及关卡中获得的技能打造喜好的流派玩法外，玩家还需在作为据点的「定海神珍铁 」中通过许多方式不断加强、培育自身能力，方能在充满神怪的山海经世界中对抗强大的对手、无往不利！
天赋
除了解锁天赋以提升、习得各种能力外，还有可增加购买物品等有助于冒险的项目。
神性技
山海经的世界中存在许多灵兽。击败灵兽后即可获得神性技，包含回复、破防、加强位移等多种技能。如何搭配及运用神性技是冒险的一大重点！
炼器
玩家可通过「炼器」制作附带各种能力的饰品、改造武器以提高攻击力、防御力；亦可在此替武器及饰品提升等级。
星河阵
与各个关卡中的怪物们战斗，有时可获得「灵玉」。灵玉可在「星河阵」中学习各种不同类型的强化效果，可在战斗中带来许多帮助！

《定海》将于 12 月 3 日于 STEAM 正式发售，而DEMO版也已于日前发布。玩家在DEMO版中的游玩纪录可完全继承到正式版游戏中。欢迎玩家一游奇幻壮丽的山海经世界！

members.title: 触乐夜话：没想到丢账号这种事也发生在我身上

news.body:
世界以痛待我，我以待以待。
前段时间，我可算是遭遇了一件对我来说堪称天塌了的大事：我发现我玩了数年的《最终幻想14》（下文简称《FF14》）账号，竟然没了。
作为一款已经运营了十多年的网游，《FF14》自然积累了相当庞大的内容，而我也在其中投入了难以计数的时间。如今，游戏已进入7.0版本的末期，而我出于各种原因，已经有一段时间没有打开过它了。
直到最近，随着8.0版本逐渐临近，相关消息越来越多，我身边那些还在关注《FF14》的朋友也开始变得“躁动”起来。
毕竟，在我们看来，最近两个大版本的表现简直称得上灾难，大家平时没少对着游戏破口大骂。甚至最近一段时间本游的知名笑话是，商城推出了一个可以精准跳过这两个“大粪”版本的剧情直通包，售价只需19元。所以可以说，就连官方自己都知道它们真的很糟糕……
但骂归骂，面对即将到来的新版本，大家多少还是抱有一点期待。也许这次真的不一样呢？
在看完新的预告片后，我的兴趣也大涨，准备重新回到艾欧泽亚，为新版本的到来做些准备。结果，当我兴冲冲地准备登录游戏时，我发现我的账号出于一些手机号和认证原因，不可抗力地再也无法登录了。
那天，我基本上就是在微信里对着朋友各种鬼哭狼嚎。
MMO玩久了，账号里攒下的东西根本没法用几句话概括。我在里面投入了小几千小时，每天吭哧吭哧地做着重复劳动，就为了一些坐骑和武器外观，还有那些倾注了不少精力的高难副本，全都随着账号的消失付诸东流。更不用说这些年来我往里面花的真金白银。
和客服来回沟通确认彻底没戏后，正常来说，事情发展到这，我或许应该顺势彻底退坑。反正已经这么久没玩了，旧账号又找不回来，正好给自己一个不再回去的理由。
当然，如果真就这么放弃，我也不会在这里写这篇文章了。
在经历了一天的短暂崩溃后，我决心从头再来，把失去的东西都夺回来。甚至因为原本所在的大区已经不开放新账号注册，我直接购入了一个新号，准备再一次从头跑起。
我这么愿意折腾，难道是因为《FF14》特别好玩吗？我实在没办法理直气壮地讲出这句话。这游戏的缺点简直骂都骂不完——无论是大多数如“通马桶”般枯燥的任务流程、令人血压升高的剧情，还是让人无法理解的技改内容，槽点多到简直数不过来。
但我也得承认，它确实给我带来了许多非常美好的回忆。还记得在5.X版本，我才真正体会到了这款游戏的美妙之处。当时的我一路玩到了凌晨5点，到达了一个新的副本。这个时间点，大部分玩家早已睡觉，想要匹配到其他人自然十分困难。但我会和朋友说哪怕要在这里再等3个小时，我也一定要排进去打完再睡觉。而到了6.0版本推出的第一分钟，我和朋友一起上线开始游玩。接下来的3天里，我们几乎没怎么睡觉，一直泡在游戏里推进主线；等到故事快要结束的时候，我们俩在语音里哭得一把鼻涕一把泪，几乎连话都讲不出来。
直到今天，这仍然是我最难忘的游戏经历之一。除此之外，我也在游戏里认识了不少人，而《FF14》那个有些奇妙的玩家社区，也总能冒出些有意思的人和事。
所以当这次新版本要出的时候，我还是和一起通宵打6.0的朋友约好，要第一时间一起上线体验。为了这一点，哪怕是重新练一个账号我也愿意。
在应聘触乐时，我被问到自己最喜欢的3个游戏，我没怎么犹豫就写出了答案，《FF14》也占有一席之地。对此，我既惊讶又不惊讶。它对我来说真的算得上“爱之深，恨之切”。我能毫不犹豫地列出它的一大堆缺点，也确实因此离开过很长一段时间。可即便刚刚痛失了多年的心血，我还是挺惊讶于自己竟然能这么快就决定重来，准备开启一段可能又要持续数千小时的冒险。
我只希望，自己都这么努力了，8.0能不要再让我吃到一坨大的……

news.title: Opinion: Grand Theft Auto VI and World of Warcraft: Forever show that mundanity is having a moment
news.summary_raw: Two of the year's biggest hits tell us that downtime and doldrums can be as compelling as dungeons and dragons.

members.title: Opinion: Grand Theft Auto VI and World of Warcraft: Forever show that mundanity is having a moment

news.body:
Opinion: Grand Theft Auto VI and World of Warcraft: Forever show that mundanity is having a moment
Two of the year's biggest hits tell us that downtime and doldrums can be as compelling as dungeons and dragons.
It's been 20 years since I last played Blizzard Entertainment's World of Warcraft. But when my friend group cajoled me into picking up World of Warcraft: Forever, I finally broke down and embraced the nostalgia of returning to the Azeroth of my youth. I rolled a Retribution Paladin, just as I did before. I raced to cut down Kobolds and Defias Bandits, feeling old instincts come alive. I was ready to set out on my grand adventure and see every fantastic quest, and every interesting new quality-of-life update that's been added to Blizzard's unprecedented revival experiment.
Then two hours later, I was in the Deeprun Tram. Waiting for a train. For the full 72 seconds. It felt like ten minutes. And I thought to myself "wait, is this supposed to be fun?"
But of course it is. Just like sitting by the campfire for a minute to get skill bonuses is fun. Just like waiting for my friends to arrive at a dungeon is fun. And just like running through a city with no speed buffs is fun. I'd forgotten that in 2004, before the UX of so many games became about supercharging dopamine hits as fast as possible, building worlds so large that waiting was on some level, necessary, was an awe-inspiring feat.
It's tempting to write this off as nostalgia for a simpler time. But a funny thing happened: Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI came out. And before the game was even out, I was learning how players were people meticulously painting the walls of a house, building IKEA furniture, and putting coffee cups in the sink.
"That's weird," I thought. "All I saw in Grand Theft Auto V was shooting and driving." But in the years since my out-of-work roommate and I lazed about playing GTA V, Rockstar Games had experimented with wild simulation technology in Red Dead Redemption 2. Now here it is in full display, bringing the little tasks of modern life to big-budget gameplay.
Two examples doesn't make for a trend, but two high-profile, massively successful examples is worth calling my shot: both of these games are telling us something important: players don't just need to be cajoled through bright likes, juicy animation, and over-signaled level design. They want to relax with life's simple pleasures—they just don't want doing so to feel as frustrating as it can in the real world.
What makes these games' chores so interesting?
Metaverse boosters from 2021-2022 may be frothing at the mouth at this trend. They worked so hard to bring the real world to the digital one, and players roundly rejected them. "Why won't people live in our digital worlds?" they ask.
The best answer comes from YouTube essayist Dan Olson, who broke down how so much Metaverse design theory recreated the friction of the real world that our brains are usually good at scrubbing out. But games are played either on 2D monitors or 3D VR headsets, and recreating this friction has narrow appeal, especially when it risks making players ask "why am I spending my free time doing things I have to do in real life?"
The key word there is "have to do." WoW: Forever and GTA VI carefully limit the mandatories of their mundane moments, and have each clearly tested how much friction their players are willing to tolerate. Observe in GTA VI how the wall-painting minigame doesn't require you to deal with the annoyance of laying out paint tarp. Its furniture-building experience doesn't force you to combine physical dexterity and hand-eye coordination with complex instructions.
Image via Blizzard Entertainment/Xbox
The chores of WoW: Forever also spotlight how pleasant UX experiences can substitute real-life frustration and make the act of standing still and waiting for time to pass a purer moment. On the one hand, I'm annoyed when I need 60 seconds to turn 100 linen cloth into bandages. On the other hand, the little "wuh-wuhmp" noise that accompanies each act is music to my ears. Same goes for the sizzling of smelting minerals. And the "clank" of blacksmithing weapons and armor.
But hark—I hear another class of game developers banging on my window. "We've been doing this for ages!" they shout. "We know players love this!" Fear not my friends, because indeed, we must talk about how this groundwork was laid by the hundreds of developers in the simulation genre.
The simulation genre has long served this need
In the last few years you've probably read many articles about the phenomenon of players enjoying "games as work," that describe how these games serve needs not being met by our real-life jobs under capitalism. I'll let critics like Cameron Kunzleman, Steph Coelho, and Michael Piantini tell you more about that. I'm certainly familiar with this dynamic—one of my favorite games in 2025 was News Tower, where I acted as editor-in-chief for a premiere paper in New York City. As if I didn't have enough angry people criticizing my writing at my day job.
But simulation design isn't just about identifying what players want to do, it's dialing in how they do it. And these studios have cooked up such a spectrum of design ideas. We have game store simulators to scratch the itch of opening packs. We have fishing games for real-life fisherman to play in the off-season. We have the entire European constellation of vehicle simulation games, which I can't even begin to wrap my head around because why on earth is a game where you drive a bus on long, real-life roadways so popular???
I'll even tip my cap to the Cozy Lives/Free Lives team's recent title Dressmaker, which has a larger narrative layer that might obscure its simulation strengths. People are going above and beyond with the game's crafting prompts, not just making dresses for the in-game characters, but for each other.
We must also consider the promotional ecosystem that benefits these titles. Simulation games benefit from what I call my "greater theory of games as instruments." Content creators live and die by performing for their audiences, and the structured tasks of these games create opportunities for streamers, YouTubers, and TikTokers to organically struggle and fail with in a way that's entertaining for viewers.
The developers of these games have known that real life is inherently interesting—and that you need to identify what's fun about it to ensure your game finds its audience.
It's not enough to copy big games
Before we go, I wish to ask readers to not let history repeat itself. Because while the simulation genre has steadily innovated and experimented in the background, WoW: Forever and GTA VI are two games that share one infamous quality: their success has infamously become the jagged rocks that fast-followers and supposed "killers" crash themselves on, and it is dangerous to copy their success for the sake of copying.
We know this merely by looking at history. Developers who survived the MMO boom and bust of the 2000s, and recent tales of studios trying to build GTA-sized games without the knowledge, best practices, or proper staffing. Even though these little mechanics are not inherently going to doom any particular game, the risk of copying them for copying's sake, treating them as some kind of "solved problem" is the foundation for bad design and business practices that will have us all saying aloud "all of this has happened before, all of us will happen again."
I even spoke with a veteran developer about this topic last week—a developer who himself is trying to make a new game that independently captures some of what makes GTA VI so special. We'd been discussing how it's not enough to have great ideas, and how the frustration and grind of making a game teaches you what players will actually enjoy. His experience in life and game development helped him sum it up in a way I found more more meaningful than just treating this as an exercise in copying mechanics.
"I find life itself to be inherently interesting," he told me. "You don't always have to be the big hero saving the world."

members.title: "You are still taking 100% of the risk" – Why Cairn dev The Game Bakers backs self-publishing for all but the smallest developers

news.body:
"You are still taking 100% of the risk" – Why Cairn dev The Game Bakers backs self-publishing for all but the smallest developers
Audrey Leprince on the value of building your own community and keeping more of the money – but working with partners when it makes sense
Self-publishing is now firmly established as a viable route to market for indie developers, with many only looking to publishers for help with specific issues – chiefly marketing, based on conversations with GamesIndustry.biz this year. Audrey Leprince, co-founder of Cairn developer The Game Bakers, argues that while working with third parties is essential, self-publishing is ultimately the only route to sustainability for indie developers.
Leprince was speaking at Paris Game Biz in October, where she gave a presentation called "Self-Publishing: Build Your Own Distribution". In addition to co-founding the Montpellier-based studio behind the indie hits Squids, Furi, Haven, and this year's Cairn, she is the co-founder of Wings, which funds games from studios with women or gender-marginalised developers in leadership roles.
Leprince talked about her experience of self-publishing with The Game Bakers, emphasising the importance of building a community around your studio, the benefits of not being financially beholden to a publisher, and the importance of continually marketing your games. Below is a summary of the key insights from her presentation.
Community connection
"The first reason I think self-publishing is fantastic is because you have this direct connection with your community," Leprince told the audience at Paris Game Biz.
"Players find their games through their communities, their friends, their family, their favourite streamer, their YouTuber – that's how they find their games. So if you are going to give your game [to a] publisher, they're going to reach them through their social media, through their outreach, through their brand, through their social media manager and community managers. And you're not going to gain access to that community [...] for the next game if you don't have the same publisher."
That direct connection builds over time. Leprince noted that around 3.8 million people played Furi and another two million played Haven, "so now we're talking to a few million people every time we launch a game."
She emphasised just how important communities are for a game's success. "They're actually the number one marketing tool," she said. "Of course, there's also the platforms, Steam, PlayStation, and Nintendo Switch, but those ones you can't really influence anymore." As an indie developer, she said, "long gone is the time where you could actually negotiate to be placed on those stores," adding that the recent move away from manual curation on Steam means your game will only be shown to specific audiences that Steam decides on. "So the community is really the number one."
Money
Leprince said that the second reason for choosing self-publishing – as well as self-funding – is that as a developer, you get to keep all the money.
She emphasised that a funding deal that sees a studio giving up 50% of their game's revenue might enable the studio to put out its first game, but even if it's a fairly big success, there may only be just enough left to make the second game – and probably not enough to do a more ambitious project. This can lock the developer into a cycle of reliance.
"The moment you choose to work with a publisher, you set your step to work with the publisher again and again and again, until you have massive success. You never have enough money to take all the risks you need if you keep giving 70% or 50% of your revenue to the publisher."
Self-funding allows a studio to retain its creative freedom and set the studio's direction, she said. "Unless you know how to find the right publisher to support the risk for your projects, you might reach a stage of your studio life where you want to make a game that no one wants to buy – that's going to be a problem. Then you're going to start making a game that people want to buy, which is not the game you wanted to make. And maybe you will be less good at making it.
"It's why I think our games are successful and quite different: It's because no one is telling us what to do."
She gave the example of how people dismissed The Game Bakers' vision for Cairn. "I swear when I said it's just about climbing, people were laughing. They thought I was joking. They were like, yeah, there's going to be boss fights or something. No, it's just climbing the mountain. They didn't believe it."
Marketing
Leprince emphasised the importance of marketing as being the key to success in self-publishing, even if it feels like an onerous task.
"We keep hearing, 'Oh yeah, but I don't have time to do marketing and publishing, because I have to work on the game'. Fair enough. But my take is that you are actually doing the marketing when you work on the game."
She explained that in making a game, the studio should have already thought deeply about things like the game's style, its audience, and what makes it different – all key marketing points.
"If you don't know what's marketable, don't make a game," she said. "You have to know who you're talking to, and what you're making, and who's your competition. It's impossible otherwise. There's no world in which you make a game and someone else is going to make it a success. It's not going to happen. You have to make it a success from the beginning, from the decisions you take, from the art director you hire, from the writer you hire, from the gameplay decisions you make from the very beginning. You are the creative director of the game. You are the first marketer of the game."
"There's no world in which you make a game and someone else is going to make it a success"
Leprince emphasised the need for developers to keep up to date on industry trends through newsletters like GameDiscoverCo, as well as engaging with the community. "There's no secret," she said. "The secret that publishers have and that you don't is that they own communities."
At the start, Leprince took on all the marketing for The Game Bakers, but now the studio has a full-time marketing manager as well as a community manager who works two days a week, creating content for sites like TikTok and Instagram. In addition, the studio works with marketing agencies.
Leprince emphasised that although it's necessary to allocate budget to marketing, there are ways to keep costs down, such as the payments to influencers. "We start organic, but what we do is we target the influencers that the big influencers watch," she said. "So we get the small ones that influence the big ones, and the big ones, when five of their friends have been playing a game, they're considering it. So that's how we got huge names in influence to cover Cairn for free."
Always on
Some may have a perception that marketing only starts near a game's launch and ends not long after, but Leprince emphasised that it remains a constant, even for games that have been out for years. "Our games have an incredible long tail. A lot of our sales come from year two, year three, year four, year five, year ten," she said.
The marketing never really stops – and the team's marketing manager is working constantly, even if the studio's next big game is still a long way from launch or even reveal. In the meantime, there are patches, DLC, and console ports to market, as well as things like awards to enter. "You have to keep pushing and talking to the community, creating events."
Leprince gave the example of a recent deep discount on Furi and Haven on Steam, which brought "massive income" to the studio, and which resulted from a discussion with Steam at GDC. "So you have a lot of ways to keep your current game selling," she said, listing things like updates to years-old titles. "All of that is marketing work. It's not production driven anymore. Then there's the art books, and merchandise, and events, all of that to keep talking about the game all the time. So it's a lot of work actually."
She said that certain events will involve big marketing pushes, like a new game mode, launch date announcement, or DLC launch, but for others, it's fine to reuse assets, or perhaps do interviews with the design or writing team. "You just have to find ways to create content as cheap as you can," she said. "Reuse everything you do. And actually they don't really mind. For instance, Nintendo doesn't mind that the trailer we put in Nintendo Direct is the same as the launch trailer."
The right partner
Even though The Game Bakers is firmly behind self-publishing and self-funding, Leprince stressed the importance of finding partners. "For Furi, PlayStation was our partner. They brought $1 million to make the game. It was against one of those deals [for] PlayStation Plus at the time."
PlayStation was also a partner for Cairn, but The Game Bakers decided they didn't want to do a subscription deal this time around. "So instead we had what we call a co-publishing deal. So they brought a substantial amount of money for marketing. They bought some placement on the store, they bought some placement in social media."
"I would say that anyway, you are still taking 100% of the risk, even if you have a publisher, because if everything fails, it's going to be on you."
Platform partners are great for providing visibility, she said. "A show like Summer Game Fest is 50 million people watching. A PlayStation showcase can go to 80 million people watching. This is not direct conversion to wishlists or sales, but it's huge awareness."
Having a partner is half of Game Bakers' marketing strategy, she said. "Without PlayStation and without Xbox, we wouldn't be where we're at. We have massive powerhouses that carry our IP much further than we could. So I advise you to always work with a more powerful partner, a platform in particular, and choose the right one."

members.title: How To Model & Texture PS1-Style Character In Blender

news.body:
How To Model & Texture PS1-Style Character In Blender
TomGrave3D shared a video walking through his design choices and overall workflow.
While we're no longer held back by the hardware limitations of the past, plenty of people still love that old-school look. Whether it's the performance benefits, the focus on art direction, or simply personal preference, PS1-style visuals are still pretty popular. And while they might look simple, recreating that style isn't always as easy as you'd think.
TomGrave3D recently put together a video showing how he created a PS1-inspired character in Blender, walking through his thought process, design choices, and overall workflow:
He also points out that this isn't meant to be a strict step-by-step tutorial, but rather a look at an approach to creating characters in this style. The video covers setting up reference images and blocking out the character, UV unwrapping, and texturing. You can find the final model and project files on the artist's Patreon.
If you're interested in creating PS1-style projects, Fawkek has a handy one-click solution for retro-style rendering with plenty of customizable options to help you get the look you want. Puck's Pixelizer is another nice tool for adding a retro touch to your 3D models. Godot developers might want to check out Calin P's breakdown of how PS1 graphics work, along with a free shader you can use in your own projects. Similarly, Unreal Engine developers might want to try Kordan's Classic Station Lighting or EvilReFlex's tools.
We also highly recommend visiting Alfred Baudisch's interactive archive of assets from PlayStation, Nintendo 64, and Sega Saturn games: it's a great resource for studying references from classic games.

features.body:
# #2 游戏的高度严肃性

玩是谦恭，不是解放

本文在腾云公众号发布时，名字为《游戏的态度：如果不“严肃”，你就无法感受它的魅力》



### 引子

*有一种错觉是，游戏之所以吸引人，是因为你可以在游戏世界里“为所欲为”。但事实恰恰相反，游戏的迷人之处，正是因为它的规则性，或者说“限制性”。*

*另一个错觉是，因为游戏太“真实”，所以人们才心甘情愿“陷”在其中。事实上，和看电影类似，人们是主动选择将自己置身于一种“假信”的状态，并以此感受其中的乐趣。*

*这些“错觉”的存在，恰恰说明了“游戏”和“严肃”如影随形。*

*而“严肃”或许是最好的“游戏态度”。*

### 00 孩子教给大人的事

> “我想要把这本书献给我六岁的儿子山姆......**他教会了我以严肃的态度看待并体验游戏，让我自始至终都乐在其中。”**【1】

在《游戏改变学习：游戏素养、批判性思维与未来教育》一书的序言中，美国著名语言学学者詹姆斯·保罗·吉这样感谢他六岁的儿子。

以严肃的态度来看待游戏，许多人都可以理解，但是“以严肃的态度来体验游戏”，这是什么意思？

在游戏中，严肃与玩乐相伴而行，形成一种辨证的诡辞（dialectic paradox），在限制与自由、谦恭与解放之间，“严肃”就像是一个捉摸不透却总是处处闪现的“幽灵”，总想摆脱人们对它的思考和定义。

让我们从游戏的“严肃性”谈起。

### 01 **没有严肃性就没有游戏**

> 没有比游戏更严肃的事【2】。—— 法国哲学家亨利·列斐伏尔

这种说法乍听起来有些不可思议。但我甚至要说：“严肃性”才是游戏成立的基础。这里的“严肃”指的是一种游戏者的心态，一种“假装”(make-believe)。

举例来说，当我们与孩子玩耍时，会假装看不见蹩脚地躲在窗帘背后的孩子；我们在踢球的时候，会假装与对方是对抗的敌人；动物们在追逐嬉戏的时候，即便不会伤害对方，也会装作在捕猎而轻咬打闹。

荷兰文化史学家赫伊津哈在《游戏的人》中也举了一个让人印象深刻的例子：“一位父亲发现四岁的儿子坐在一排椅子的前端玩‘开火车’游戏。他拥抱儿子的时候，男孩说：‘别亲火车头，爸爸，不然车厢就知道它不是真的了。’ ”【3】

**每个孩子都心知肚明他“只是在假装（only-pretending）”，但这种“假装”绝不是一种不严肃的态度。这种假装实际上是一种对于规则的认可，对于游戏某种虚构本质视而不见却又沉浸其中的态度的“严肃”，才能让这个游戏进行下去。**



人类学家罗杰凯瓦卢（Roger Caillois）将其称之为假装Make-Believe，一种与现实相对应的非现实性/第二现实的特殊态度。【4】

哲学家伯纳尔·舒兹在《蚱蜢：游戏，生命与乌托邦》中则将其称之为“游戏态度（Lusory attitude，拉丁文ludus，意指游戏）”，指这样一种“奇异”的状态：人们接受游戏规则限制采取效率低下的方法，而非用直接且高效的方式来达成目标。【5】

**这种假装与严肃的态度还体现在对游戏规则的遵守。**

游戏都有前游戏目标（Pre-lusory Goal），例如四百米赛跑，目标就是从起点跑到终点；同时有我们要遵守的规则（Constitutive Rules），我们并不能骑着自行车去拿长跑第一名，或者是开着作弊器违反规则通关游戏之后说——我赢了！因为你在违反规则，或者说参与游戏的这种"假装"的时候，你已经离开了游戏。



**因此，游戏绝不仅仅是嬉皮笑脸、毫无规矩。事实恰恰相反。**

荷兰语言学家赫伊津哈一直把“扫兴的人”作为理解游戏意义的关键。所谓“扫兴的人”，就是那些触犯规则、无视规则的人，这样的搅局者（spoil-sport）褫夺了游戏的幻觉，也是游戏者最反感的。

举例来说，在餐桌上行酒令，输了游戏却不愿接受惩罚的人一定会被人“看扁”；下棋的时候，我们也不愿意和那些违反“落棋无悔”规则的人下棋；看直播的时候，我们对于开挂者和作弊者的愤怒，对于假赛和不全力以赴之人的鄙视......都说明游戏里的“搅局者”是不受欢迎的。

**由此我们也可以发现，游戏的意义与魅力并不在于人们通常认为的“自由”或是“解放”，而恰恰是在于游戏本身的“限制条件”，在于游戏使人必须“遵守规则”。**

这是“游戏”与“玩”的悖论：“乐趣源于对自由的限制而不是对自由的放纵。【6】”

### 02 **假信：游戏和艺术的“异曲同工”**

可别小瞧这种“严肃性”与“假装”。这样的态度不仅仅存在于孩子们搭沙堡、过家家游戏中，同样和审美/艺术相关联。

“小男孩将一根木棍当作木马，假装在骑马以获取乐趣。”在《木马沉思录》中，艺术史家贡布里希著名以这种“假信”为起点，探究所有艺术形式的根源。

这种“假信”的态度可以在很多艺术形式的审美中找到。

例如，对于文学作品的欣赏，有一种被称之为“怀疑搁置(suspension of disbelief)”的状态。这一概念由诗人塞缪尔·泰勒·柯尔律治所创造，指的是读者主动接受故事荒谬或在现实世界中“不可能”的地方【7】，并享受其中。如何理解？

**你可以想象一下，如果你在阅读奇幻小说时忍不住去质疑“世界上哪有这么大的龙？”“怎么可能有人脱水了还能活着？”等这些场景的“荒谬”，那么你可能会与《权力的游戏》或《三体》等作品中最震撼人心的场景失之交臂。因为你不愿意让自己处于“假信”的状态。**

同理，演员的专业表演、固定的座椅、安静的空间...电影院或剧院的这些规则，都是为了让观众忘记现实，沉浸在导演营造的叙事中。

这种在电影院中仿佛置身另一个世界而假装忘记现实的体验是十分重要的。这也是为什么大卫林奇认为，倘若在手机上播放电影，那么“一万年也无法体验电影”。【8】

一旦这种“假信”的状态被“揭穿”，在场的所有人就会从陶醉的美梦中惊醒——打破了尼采所说的观众的施魔(Verzauberung)。美妙的体验便瞬间消失。



> 玩是谦恭，不是解放。——伊恩·博格斯特（Ian Bogost）

**更进一步说，游戏规则之下的“严肃性”和“假装”中蕴含着一种对于事物的“尊重感”。**

玩家心甘情愿接受这些规则，进入这个游戏所创造的魔圈（magic circle）之中；观众同样仿佛都约定好了似的，进入电影和戏剧“不真实”的世界里。在这种状态中，人不再是以自己为中心，而是去接受事物本身的设置，去倾听艺术的声音，去接受艺术作品。

也就是说，人们心甘情愿地放下自我为中心的主体地位，而与处于客体的事物共同游戏。

在电影院里，与被“固定”在座椅上、不能随意移动、不能大声说话的观影者相比，电影本身反而成为了一个“行动者”，它仿佛在用自身的光影刺向身处黑暗中的观众，让他们被触动（affected）。【9】

**也就是说，自认为最具有能动性（agency）的人类，在电影院中恰恰不是特别“有生气”（vibrant）。如果从“非人类中心主义”的视角来看，事实确实如此。**



电子游戏也是如此。

玩家需要主动放弃自己身体的运动，放弃多余的感知方式，去接受一个由游戏设计师设定好的、由交互与反馈构成的“角色替身”（avatar）。当然，还有那些游戏世界中的复杂规则。

在这样的限制中，当玩家的操作变得越来越娴熟，他就能够感受到动作游戏中操作的美感，感受到游戏中的角色就像玩家感官和身体的延伸。一种虚拟的运动感（kinesthesia）与本体感受（proprioception）【10】被构建出来。

表面上，游戏角色是被玩家所操控的，但实际上，玩家也受着游戏和角色的限制——游戏角色或游戏成为一种具有自己生命力的主体，一种“拟生命”(quasi-life)，反过来限制和操控着玩家。【11】

**玩家在这样对限制的接受和发挥、被动与主动、操控与反操控之间，感受到游戏的美感与乐趣。**

从这个角度出发，或许就可以理解为什么哲学家伽达默尔将 “游戏作为艺术作品的存在方式”。因为游戏/艺术不再是一个对象化的客体，而成为卷入游戏者的主体，被动而却又含有主动性的意义(der mediale sinn)。

这也是为什么说游戏和艺术有异曲同工之处。

因为游戏和所有艺术的运作方式，都涉及到观众/玩家的一种“参与限制”又“超越限制”的审美状态。事实上，只有这样才能感受到美的存在。当然，这里也涉及到现代人应该具备的一种能力：一种能够沉浸在事物之中，遵守规则而体会事物的规律与美好之处的能力。

### 03 **辩证的游戏态度：“无用”游戏的魔法**

> “或许一个人如果想体会到生活中的浪漫情调就必须在某种程度上是一个演员；而要想跳出自身之外，则必须能够对自己的行动抱着一种既超然物外又沉浸于其中的兴趣。” —— 毛姆

前文说游戏的成立核心在于严肃的遵守规则、接受限制而追逐目标、沉浸在游戏之中。但当游戏结束，我们其实都明白：它只是一场游戏，It's just for fun（这只是为了开心），it's not real（这并不是真的）。

**玩游戏的人知道自己在玩游戏。**玩游戏的人知道它的结果其实并不重要，它是“无意义”的，Roger Caillois将其定义为非生产性的（Unproductive）。

简单来说：游戏本质上是“无用”的。

游戏要达成的目标是没有意义且微不足道的（例如把高尔夫球放进洞里，或者是电子游戏这样的干脆虚构出来的目标）。

有些人对于大部分游戏不感兴趣，或者说，提不起兴趣，很大的原因就来自于这里，他们用功利主义或目标论的标准来看游戏，游戏就是完全无意义的。

但奇特的辩证法就在于此，参与游戏中的人们并不是因为游戏的目标十分重要，或者游戏可以给自己带来什么样的好处去玩游戏，而仅仅因为游戏的过程中的体验。他们愿意进行严肃的参与，愿意去做这样的一件在寻常价值体系下毫无价值的事情。而这往往就是乐趣和意义的魔法发生的地方。

**这里所提倡的是一种辨证的游戏态度，超然物外而又沉浸其中。**

相反的，当很多人误把游戏的目标当做游戏的价值，为了得到某些游戏内的数值，达到某个段位，为了游戏的目标（实际上是微不足道的）而废寝忘食，醒悟过来后发现这些目标对现实没有任何价值（当然了，这就是游戏的特点）。

如果当我们只是一心为了游戏中虚构的目标而努力，忽略了过程。亦或在过程中没有感到丝毫乐趣却依旧在重复性地游玩，那我们并不在游戏，而在工作与劳作。



###

### 04 **缺乏游戏态度的现代人**

当你因游戏而忘了吃饭时间，你的母亲或许会感到不理解，而你也很难向她作出解释。

这是因为，你们之间存在一个错位：

母亲所看到的是游戏这项活动的非必要性/非生产性的一面——即“游戏只不过是游戏”；而此时，她的孩子正全心全意正扑在游戏中——他暂时忘记了“现实”，他正灵活运用这游戏世界中的符号，符号背后是他与九个真实的人在先前的三十分钟里的投入，所以**他对此十分严肃——而这也正是游戏得以成立与展开的基础，也是这个孩子能够进行游戏，并享受游戏乐趣的基本条件与要求**。

这或许是现在的整个社会上对电子游戏存在的错位。

游戏玩家的游戏态度让其投入其中，但有些人过了头沉迷游戏，而那些站在电子游戏外部的人困惑并对这种社会现象指指点点，他们并不能投入其中，也并没有玩游戏的能力。

想要学会玩游戏并不是那么简单的。

这里首先需要一种游戏素养（Game literacy），也就是接受一套新的规则，一套新的符号系统并且灵活运用的能力。

就像《游戏设计之快乐理论》或者是许多游戏设计者和思考者将游戏看作是对于某种模式（pattern）的学习一样，《游戏改变学习》一书中将游戏的过程其称之为批判式的学习。前提在于，首先我们要主动，且自愿地面对游戏提供给的一种新的学习以及思维方式，要自愿地去接受一套规则。【12】

好比一个从来没有接触过《英雄联盟》的玩家，它需要学习游戏中的上百个英雄，记住其对应的技能形象，出装，并且能够在学习中逐渐把握到整体游戏战场节奏的变化，用书中的话来说：“学会用新视角来定位词语/图像/标识/物品等事物的意义，建立新联系。”

还有一种最重要的态度，也就是这篇文章谈论的：

在生活和工作节奏如此快速的今天，我们能够保有一种不“功利”的态度，在认识到游戏“目标无用”的前提下，花时间去严肃和真诚地做“无用之事”，这本身就是珍贵的。这需要一种对事物本身的好奇，对创造物与艺术品的尊重和投入，更需要不凡的创造力。

**“世间最肤浅的莫过于以浅薄的姿态面对正经事，世间最引人入胜的莫过于对待琐事的事后显示出你之所为绝非琐事。”** 伊拉斯谟在他的传世名篇《愚人颂》的开头这样写道。

或许玩亦是自制、亦是自由，如同玩家可主动接受游戏的规则限制与他人共享乐趣，亦可跳脱出来进行批判性思考，将游戏看做一个系统、一个被设计的空间，进行再创造和超越，并评判游戏的好坏。那就有待下篇文章去扩展了【13】

features.title: Keys to Combat Design: Anatomy of an Attack
features.title_cn: 战斗设计要点：拆解一次攻击的构成
features.editor_note: 来自现有收藏；讨论攻击动作的分段与战斗设计。
features.body:
Welcome to the next article on a series dedicated to Combat Design! It all started with one article, but it quickly became apparent that this topic is way too wide and complex to be able to tackle it with a single one.
This series is the logical succession of the article Keys to Rational Enemy Design, so make sure you check it out.
In this series, we will talk about all the components that a designer needs to consider to produce a snappy, meaningful, rewarding, skill-based fight:
- Pacing
- Enemy AI and decision trees
- Group AI
- Player’s abilities and metrics
- Player’s strategies
- Difficulty management and rationalization
- Hitboxes and Hurtboxes
- …
- And, of course, attacks, our topic of the day.
We are starting this series with this topic because attacks are the most core component of a fight. Dissecting what makes up an attack, both for the player and for the enemies the player is fighting will put in light the keys to a good fight: readability, fairness, skill, challenge, purpose…
We will talk about the different phases of an attack, about Windows of Opportunity (or WoO in short), about animation, about input lag… And, hopefully, you will have at the end of this article all the keys to challenge your own fight system and recognize the elements that make games like Hollow Knight or Nioh so good in that domain.
But before we start, it’s important to understand the scope of what we will discuss: by combat, we mean any real-time armed confrontation between the player and one or more enemies. Our study will then be independent of said weapons, being fists, melee weapons, or ranged weapons. Street Fighter, Punch-Out, For Honor, Assassin’s Creed, Hollow Knight, Cuphead, Mordhau, Dark Soul… Every one of these games confronts the player using globally the same design rules, and these are the ones we will break down today, starting with the enemy’s side of it.
Enemy’s Attacks
In order to properly design an attack, we first need to understand what phases compose an attack. An enemy attack is on paper very straightforward, and always made of three distinct elements:
Think of it as in real life: should you want to throw a kick, you will first start preparing your body for it, bending your body backward, and arming your leg. This is the anticipation. Then comes the attack, the very small part that is about hitting the opponent. Finally, once the attack finishes, your body will have to go to its final resting position (that could be the original one): this is the recovery.
Well, attacks in video games work in the exact same way:
One reason is of course because our players, though playing in a fictional world, expect real-life constraints and forces to apply in it too: gravity, weight, anatomy, physiology… But we will come to that when talking about animation.
Another reason, and one that is particularly interesting for us game designers, is that these three phases are critical for the gameplay, each one of them in its own way. They are the base for players’ tactics to emerge and are carefully crafted to balance difficulty, challenge abilities, and drive playstyles.
Let’s develop each of them using the player experience as the common thread of this article.
Key #1: Every single attack should be broken down into 3 phases: Anticipation, Attack, and Recovery.
Anticipation
The anticipation of an attack is, in essence, a Sign for the player that a specific attack is coming (see. Keys to Signs & Feedback). It’s a warning. It will drive the player to get away before the attack happens, block, dodge, or even push his luck and try hitting the enemy to interrupt the attack.
For the anticipation phase to fill its role properly, it must comply with a few rules:
- The animation of each anticipation must be unique: no other attack from this enemy can have the same anticipation (except if you want to pull a twist on your players, who am I to judge). And by unique, I mean drastically different. Subtleties are lost in the heat of a fight, players won’t ever see that an enemy slightly changed its stance before starting a different attack, and it will ultimately lead to frustration.
- The animation of each anticipation must hint at its follow-up attack: a player shouldn’t have to rely on memorization and trial and error to learn how to defeat an enemy. The animation, just like in real life, should follow logic (for example, bringing an ax behind your body before splitting a log in two). Record and study your players’ first encounter with your enemies. Even if they get hit by an attack, they should have seen it coming and started reacting accordingly.
Key #2: an efficient Anticipation translates in a unique warning animation, telegraphing the incoming attack.
Cuphead is a beautiful reference to study. Their over-exaggerated animation style and the cartoon codes of the 1930s allowed them to really create the most legible combat animations I’ve seen in a game.
I mean… Look at that anticipation!
Now that we talked about animation unicity and continuity there is still one big point to discuss relative to the anticipation: timing. How long should this anticipation last? Or, in development terms: how many frames must the anticipation have? Well, unfortunately, there is no clear rule for that as it depends on two factors: what action do you expect the player to do (and how long does it take to do it)? And what is the extra margin you want to give them? Remember that acknowledging an incoming danger and reacting to it isn’t immediate for a human being (unfortunately).
As a rule of thumb, consider that the reaction time of a player will be 0.25 seconds (so around 8 frames in a 30fps game, and 15 frames in a 60fps one). Now let’s say you want the player to block a specific attack, and that the block will be efficient at the end of its animation, 10 frames after the press of the block button by the player. The minimum anticipation time will be 10+8= 18 frames! Of course, other variables could affect this number: the extra frames the weapon will need to reach the players based on their distance from the enemy, the input lag, etc. But you get the idea.
The difficulty of dodging/parrying/interrupting/blocking the attack will then crystallize in a single metric: how much of an extra buffer do you give your players on top of this minimum anticipation time? This part will be a constant fine-tuning between players and developers. Playtests are key.
Key #3: Anticipation time = (player’s reaction time) + (expected player’s ability trigger time) + (difficulty buffer).
Attack
The attack part is the most obvious for us to imagine as it mimics perfectly real-life scenarios. The enemy will try to use its weapon (a fist, a sword, a gun) to hit a vulnerable part of our player: usually its body. Easy enough.
That being said, there are a lot of subtleties that will make an attack feel good. What we are looking for here is a sharp, snappy feeling and not a sloppy unpredictable one.
When designing an attack, you want it to be:
- Instant
- Unambiguous
- With a clear intent
- Precise
- Driving a specific player’s reaction
It seems straight-forward enough and yet plenty of games miss the spot with these directions. Having an instant attack means that your animation must not be longer than a few frames from the end of the anticipation to the start of the recovery. This means you will probably have to bend the laws of physics slightly to exaggerate the movement. Of course, we can find plenty of examples of extremely slow, pressuring attacks but these do not change the goal we are trying to achieve: we want the player to be able to tell exactly when the attack will land. Any blurriness at that moment will result in a sloppy, frustrating attack.
Driving a specific player’s reaction and being unambiguous means that you want your attack to be pretty stereotypical and its metrics to fit the player’s abilities. For example, you do not want a wavy, diagonal attack with varying speed. Instead, you will prefer a clean horizontal swipe with a constant speed.
Look at that Yokai’s double attack from Nioh:
Remember what I was saying about bending the laws of physics? The anticipation is slow and involves the entire Yokai’s body, showcasing the insane weight (and deadly power) of that ax. Considering the struggle to lift this weapon, there is no way the demon could swing it that fast. But at that specific moment, anatomy and realism do not matter. What matters is that his swing is instant and perfectly horizontal, allowing the player to precisely time his dodge under it.
The follow-up attack follows the same principles: perfectly vertical and happening in a blink. You will notice that this attack cannot hit a player that dodged the first hit (the Yokai doesn’t reorient mid-attack). It is used either as a Window of Opportunity (WoO) for the players to land their own counter-attack or a double punishment should a player get hit by the first blow.
Key #4: an attack is instant, constant, and with a very small amount of varying parameters.
Side note: look at the anticipation. It is unique, recognizable, and without subtleties. The downside I see is how close this ax rotation is from looking like an attack. Nioh actually deals with these issues (as they are common among their enemies) by adding a VFX to the weapon during the attack phase (i.e. the dangerous part). Weapon trails are very efficient Signs and support the learning and understanding of the attacks and patterns of enemies. Plenty of games use this trick, you could consider it too!
Key #5: Adding a weapon trail VFX to all attacks, following the weapon and its hitbox, is a clean way to highlight its deadly part (and the VFX persistence will underline the attack direction).
Recovery
Finally, once an attack has been performed, comes the recovery. And let’s make it clear right away, the goal of this phase is extremely simple: give the player a clear Window of Opportunity. A window to hit back, to heal, to run away, to reload, to plan

members.title: Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

ai.body:
Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton
TL;DR
Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.
Introduction
A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.
NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.
1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab
For simulation and training, prepare:
A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.
Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.
For physical-robot testing, prepare:
A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.
A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.
A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.
Quick install
Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:
git lfs install
git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git
cd IsaacLab
uv sync --frozen
Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:
uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets
Download the walking policy
Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.
uv run isaaclab play \
--task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
--rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \
--num_envs 1 --visualizer none \
--video newton_gl --video_length 1 \
presets=backlash
2. Build the obstacle course
The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box, office bin, bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.
uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \
--repo-type dataset \
--revision 9d4556bfe80868c1d27a7a7ba1c2774e63e8cedd \
--include "box_cardboard_a01/*" \
--include "trashCan_office_black_a03/*" \
--include "table_bedside_b01/*" \
--local-dir ./assets/simready
At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.
Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.
Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.
3. Understand how ToF sensing guides the walking policy
The IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck
task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.
During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.
Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.
The obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle
. Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py
, ToF sensing is in sensors.py
, and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/
.
Model the ToF sensor
MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.
Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.
# Selected settings; mount and raycast targets omitted.
head_tof = MicroDuckToFCameraCfg(
prim_path=MICRODUCK_HEAD_BODY_PATH,
update_period=1.0 / 15.0,
pattern_cfg=patterns.PinholeCameraPatternCfg(
focal_length=1.0, width=8, height=8,
horizontal_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE,
vertical_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE,
),
randomization=ToFRandomizationCfg(
mount_pitch_degrees=(-10.0, 10.0),
mount_height_m=(-0.02, 0.02),
floor_validity_midpoint_offset_m=(0.0, 0.13),
near_floor_edge_impairment_probability=0.5,
),
data_types=["distance_to_image_plane", "distance_to_camera"],
max_distance=TOF_MAX_RANGE,
depth_clipping_behavior="zero",
)
4. Train the Microduck policy across parallel environments
Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.
The 16,384 environments shown here are configurable, not a minimum requirement. Lower --num_envs
to fit your GPU’s available memory. With fewer environments collecting experience in parallel, reaching comparable policy performance may require more training iterations and longer training time. We also trained this policy on NVIDIA DGX Spark in approximately 6 hours using 4,096 parallel environments for 3,000 PPO updates, demonstrating a smaller-scale configuration for the same workflow.
Run this command to train the policy:
uv run isaaclab train \
--task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \
--rl_library rsl_rl \
--num_envs 16384 \
--max_iterations 1500 \
--seed 42 \
--device cuda:0 \
--visualizer none \
presets=backlash
Figure 2. Parallel MicroDuck obstacle-avoidance simulation
5. Inspect behavior and export the policy to ONNX
Playback uses the same props, primitives, frozen walker and sensor randomization as training, with a different seed for new obstacle arrangements.
Navigation checkpoints are saved under logs/rsl_rl/microduck_obstacle_avoidance_tof_flat_backlash/<timestamp>/
relative to the repository root. Choose a model_<iteration>.pt
file from your run and replace /absolute/path/to/model.pt
below with its path. This plays the policy, opens the Newton viewer and records 20 seconds of simulation. Set --viz to none for headless recording.
uv run --extra video isaaclab play \
--task IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck \
--rl_library rsl_rl \
--checkpoint /absolute/path/to/model.pt \
--num_envs 1 \
--seed 6173 \
--device cuda:0 \
--viz newton_gl \
--video newton_gl \
--video_length 1000 \
presets=backlash
Playback saves TorchScript and ONNX models in the checkpoint’s exported folder. Keep the ONNX data file alongside the model.
Figure 3. Cone-course evaluation with requested motion, policy steering, and ToF input overlays.
6. Test obstacle avoidance on a real Microduck
These deployment tools run the navigation model on a laptop and send adjusted gamepad commands to the walking policy on the robot. Use the same walking policy that was used during navigation training.
Section 1 saves the walker’s ONNX export to .pretrained_checkpoints/rsl_rl/https/omniverse-content-production.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Assets/Isaac/6.2/Isaac/IsaacLab/PretrainedCheckpoints/rsl_rl/exported/policy.onnx
, relative to the Isaac Lab repository root.
Load that walking policy using Pollen’s policy-loading guide. The deployment README includes the transfer steps, including how to package an ONNX export that uses an external data file.
From your Isaac Lab checkout, set up SSH access and check inference with the robot standing upright and still:
cd scripts/deploy/microduck_tof_nav
ssh-copy-id microduck@ROBOT_HOST
uv run nav_pad.py --robot ROBOT_HOST \
--model /absolute/path/to/navigation/exported/policy.onnx \
--dry-run --seconds 30
Dry-run copies the helpers and streams sensor data, but sends no movement commands. Watch the proposed commands as obstacles enter the sensor’s view. Keep the navigation ONNX and any companion .data file together.
Once those checks pass, start supervised gamepad navigation:
uv run nav_pad.py --robot ROBOT_HOST \
--model /absolute/path/to/navigation/exported/policy.onnx
Hold the stick forward to request movement; the policy adjusts the command to avoid obstacles. Release the stick to stop, press X to toggle navigation, and use Ctrl-C to end the session. Forward speed
