The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled.
iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis.
None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply.
“Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.”
Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle.
“Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.”
What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime.
“Teams can focus on solving their business problems and delegate execution to our platform.”
The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later.
“The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time.
The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable.
Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox.
“It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.”
The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains iFood’s ecosystem requires—Python, Java, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, Rust, JavaScript, and Go—along with general-purpose tools. Beyond the sandbox, the agent can access Nexus, GitLab, Docker, Snyk, Kubernetes, and AWS.
The model choice came down to three factors considered together, rather than just one.
“We chose GPT‑5.6 Luna because, among models at the same checkpoint, the benchmarks showed it offered a great balance of intelligence, efficiency, and execution speed—how quickly it could complete tasks. Those three qualities together led us to choose GPT‑5.6 Luna.”
That balance matters more for a platform built to scale than it would for a one-off use case. With tens of thousands of tokens being consumed, the average cost of four U.S. cents per run stops being a minor detail and becomes an architectural consideration.
“Given our plans to scale the platform across many use cases at iFood, the balance of efficiency and intelligence that OpenAI’s model provides ensures we can scale sustainably.”
Delegating execution at scale creates a new challenge: automatically determining whether the agent did what it was supposed to do.
iFood’s answer comes in the step after the session. Once execution is complete, the result is processed using OpenAI’s Structured Outputs, which requires the output to conform to a predefined contract.
“We process the result using Structured Outputs, which ensures the response follows a predefined contract. From the agent’s session, we can identify the outputs within the response structure we expect. This helps reduce uncertainty and ensures we can always get a response from the agent’s session, whether positive or negative.”
The platform already powers an internal iFood security product that scans the 15,000 repositories for vulnerable dependencies and attempts to fix them.

Routine work no longer competes for the team’s attention. That leaves time for problems that require judgment.
“You can unlock those productivity gains without necessarily having to monitor the work as it happens.”
The Remote Agents Platform was designed as an internal layer with similarities to the way OpenAI makes this type of task available to external customers.
“The Remote Agents Platform drew a lot of inspiration from OpenAI’s APIs, both the Batch API and the Agents API, which is an even more recent OpenAI product. We built a platform that resembles those products, but is internal to iFood.”
The inspiration went beyond the concept. It extends to the design of the interfaces, the organization of resources, and the approach to asynchronous execution with results retrieved later.
“These products directly inspired how we built our solution.”

Beyond knowing how to answer a customer’s request, AI support agents need to be able to execute a solution. And for that, they need access to the right tools and instructions.
According to Richpanel CEO Amit RG, human support agents can use 20 or 30 tools to serve a customer, and the procedures they follow may never have been written down.
Richpanel(opens in a new window) solves that using OpenAI models to both set up the tools and procedures AI support agents need to act and handle customer conversations.
“The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it.”
Deploying a support agent often requires a forward-deployed engineer to connect the agent to a customer’s systems and define how it should work. Amit saw that many companies didn’t have engineers to spare and asked himself, “What if that forward-deployed engineer itself was an AI agent?”
So Richpanel built it: an AI manager to handle agent setup. Customers began calling it Boss AI. It writes procedures and defines how Richpanel’s frontline support agent, copilot, and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need.
Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow.
Richpanel designs the frontline agent to handle hundreds of thousands of conversations, making the cost of each interaction an important part of model selection. It uses GPT‑6 Luna and other OpenAI models for that work. Amit says Richpanel takes the same approach to its copilot and quality-assurance agents.
“What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence,” Amit says. Richpanel’s customers may already use low-cost outsourced support. Automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point.

“OpenAI models can run these long-context, longer-horizon tasks while still being very cost efficient.”
At the time of the October 2026 interview, Amit said Richpanel had completed approximately 300 AI customer-support deployments over the previous six months.

ai.body:
Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
24th November 2026
I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.
Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.
Coding agents in November 2025
Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.
In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:
Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.
This held up.
Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025.
Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant.
The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right. It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.
Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.
The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.
Fable class models in June/July
We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.
In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.
After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st.
For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models. My definition of these:
In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz
screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.
A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.
Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.
I’d currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as “cheap Fable”). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.
These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.
3D modeling and game development in September/October
Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they’ll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.
I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here’s Gemini 4 Neon’s attempt at “Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data”, for example.
3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don’t know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.
Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game. It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play.
I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!
Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 “This game isn’t fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.” And it worked. My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.
Opus 5.5 was the first model I’d used that appeared to understand fun. I’ve since worked on several little game projects where prompts like “Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful” produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.
Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I’ve been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they’d been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.
The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster.
It feels like another inflection point to me.
Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?
I’m still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.
I’m getting so much done with that model right now!
It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I’ve been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44—plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38—all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.
If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That’s a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.
Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don’t think I’ll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

ai.body:
24th November 2026 - Link Blog
GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery. Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:
With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.
Here's the digitized sketchbook.
Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.
Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:
But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

members.title: 高德发布世界模型ABot-World 0.5，支持构建音画同步、可实时重塑的AI物理世界

ai.body:
高德发布世界模型ABot-World 0.5，支持构建音画同步、可实时重塑的AI物理世界
近日，阿里巴巴集团旗下高德正式发布新一代通用交互式世界模型 ABot-World 0.5。
近日，阿里巴巴集团旗下高德正式发布新一代通用交互式世界模型 ABot-World 0.5。新版模型全面强化了真实物理反馈，不仅新增攻击、跳跃、驾驶等丰富技能，更首次支持音画同步生成，以及自然语言实时重塑世界。
凭借在物理仿真与交互能力上的全面突破，ABot-World 0.5在权威世界模型评测基准WBench上力压一众模型厂商，斩获物理性和总分第一。即日起，用户可前往交互式世界模型工坊（abot-world.amap.com）进行体验。
从视觉渲染到物理仿真，数据规模化扩展催生模型质变
当下，世界模型正经历从“视觉渲染”向“物理仿真”的范式进化，不仅需要模型还原出逼真的视觉场景，更要求它能理解并计算真实世界的运行逻辑——物理碰撞如何真实反馈、外部指令如何作用于场景等。
得益于高德自有的数据管线Phys AI Data，ABot-World 0.5从海量数据中学习了现实世界人物、事物和环境的演变，深度理解从动作执行到物理反馈的因果链，从而在物理反馈、音画同步与实时重塑三个维度完成了核心技术的跨越式迭代。
在真实物理反馈方面，全新的ABot-World 0.5依靠数据规模化扩展（Data Scaling），深度学习了刚体碰撞、柔性形变、运动惯性等物理机制。当用户在场景中操控角色移动、释放技能或与场景物体发生交互时，模型能够实时生成高度仿真的受力结果与运动轨迹。这种连续且真实的物理响应，让用户的每一次操作都能获得扎实的物理反馈。
在音画同步方面，针对以往世界模型“有画无声”，导致感官体验割裂的痛点，ABot-World 0.5将原生音频的推演直接内嵌至世界生成当中。无论是角色的步伐跳跃、载具的引擎轰鸣，还是物体间的剧烈碰撞与自然环境的风声雨声，均伴随画面实时生成，进一步贴近物理世界规律。
在实时重塑方面，相较于只能简单漫游的世界模型，ABot-World 0.5赋予了用户在世界生成过程中动态干预和导演的能力。在世界生成的同时，用户只需输入一句自然语言指令，即可动态调整剧情走向、环境气象，赋予角色全新技能，收获言出法随的操纵体验。
拓展多元应用边界，全面支持内容创作与具身智能训练
凭借真实物理反馈、原生音频与言出法随的实时重塑能力，ABot-World 0.5展现出在具身智能、影视制作和游戏开发等领域广泛的应用潜力。
在游戏开发与影视领域，创作者无需编写复杂代码或设计繁琐的分镜脚本，用一句话就能快速搭建出音画同步、物理反馈真实的开放世界原型，并实时修改互动剧情。
在具身智能领域，ABot-World 0.5已能作为核心训练载体，批量生成高度拟真的训练数据，不仅能够模拟物品抓取等刚性交互，还能够模拟叠衣服、擦桌子等复杂的柔性形变。
高德ABot-World研发负责人表示：“ABot-World 0.5的模型效果，进一步印证了数据规模化扩展在世界模型领域的决定性作用。依托高德深厚的真实世界数据积累和体系化的数据管线，我们能够源源不断地为模型注入高质量训练养料，使其对复杂物理规律的理解持续加深，并实现模型层面的能力跃升。”
据悉，ABot-World 0.5分为Iris和Halo两个版本，Iris版可直接本地部署，仅需消费级显卡即可流畅运行；Halo版则借助云端算力提供更极致的性能表现，用户可在生成式视频开发者平台Reactor上通过API调用或在线体验。

蚂蚁开源医疗健康预测模型，根据睡眠数据可预测未来六年150种疾病风险
蚂蚁刚刚发布医疗健康模型全家桶
AI在医疗健康领域的应用，正在从疾病识别、健康咨询向更长期的健康风险预测延伸。11 月 24 日，蚂蚁百灵宣布开源医疗健康预测模型 LingSante Pulse，可通过理解人体日常产生的生理信号，预测未来六年内150种疾病表型的发生风险。
不同于传统模型主要针对某一种生理信号或特定疾病进行训练，LingSante Pulse能够统一处理脑电图、心电图、光电脉搏波、肌电图等多种生理信号，并适应不同传感器的组合。模型基于超过15万小时、多场景生理序列数据预训练，能够从不同生理信号中提取人体状态特征，实现健康情况的远期预测。
在相关评测中，其可达到较高预测可靠性的疾病表型数量，比此前最优模型增加约42%。即使只使用心电图和胸带呼吸信号两个相对简单的传感器通道，模型对118种疾病仍具备较强的预测能力，接近使用完整睡眠监测设备的外部模型表现。
在其他任务中，LingSante-Pulse也展现出较强的通用性。在覆盖脑电、心电、脉搏波和肌电四大领域的38项单传感器预测任务，以及睡眠分期、睡眠呼吸暂停筛查等多模态任务评测中，模型综合表现领先现有单传感器领域专有模型及多模态生理信号基础模型。
目前，利用AI分析生理信号、开展疾病早期识别和风险预测，已经成为医疗AI领域的重要研究方向。国内外不少研究机构和企业都在探索，从心电、睡眠监测和可穿戴设备数据中发现传统诊疗中不易察觉的健康变化。
据了解，蚂蚁刚刚发布医疗健康模型全家桶，覆盖医疗推理、多模态理解、疾病风险预测、安全防护和实时智能体等多个方向。与此同时，阿福App宣布新一轮升级，解锁AI 实时音视频“望闻问切”功能，升级AI健康管家能力，并扩展无屏手环、戒指两大健康硬件品类。目前，LingSante-Pulse相关技术报告及模型已在GitHub和Hugging Face开放。
